 Hillsborough Dengue Cases Rise at Slowest Pace Since August as Cooler Weather Offers Only Partial Relief From Mosquitoes
 Published Nov 11, 2026 2:10 AM EST 
 By
 Elena Vega 
 Justin Sullivan | Getty Images 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 Hillsborough County added 22 locally acquired dengue cases in the week of Oct. 25 to 31, its smallest weekly increase since mid-August, bringing the county's total to 407 since the outbreak began in July, WUSF reported . Statewide, Florida has confirmed 524 locally acquired cases since July.
 The slowdown comes as cooler air moves into Tampa Bay. Cooler weather can make the Aedes mosquitoes that spread dengue less active, but a UF Health epidemiologist said it would take at least one night of a hard freeze to kill off their numbers.
 For households in Tampa, Brandon and St. Petersburg, that means the risk is easing but has not ended. Mosquito surveillance still shows dengue virus activity in many neighborhoods, and the county has extended its local state of emergency through Nov. 12.
 Developing Story Note: This report covers new developments involving Florida's 2026 dengue outbreak. Information may change as state and county health officials release additional findings. Case data are through Oct. 31, 2026, from the Florida Department of Health's weekly arbovirus report. Hillsborough County extended its emergency order through Nov. 12, 2026. 
 Weekly Counts Through October 31
 Weekly cases in Hillsborough peaked at 53 during Sept. 20 to 26. The latest 22 cases are the fewest since the week ending Aug. 16, when the county recorded 16. Pinellas County added 13 cases for a total of 80.
 Hillsborough and Pinellas accounted for nearly all of the state's 39 new local infections that week, with Miami-Dade and Orange counties reporting the rest. Florida has also logged 382 travel-associated cases this year, most in Miami-Dade, bringing the total number of dengue illnesses past 900.
 The scale remains historic. Florida's previous high for local cases was 199 in 2023, and the state reported 62 last year. An 80-year-old Tampa woman who died Sept. 4 was the first person in the Tampa Bay area killed by dengue in nearly a century, WUSF reported , citing a University of South Florida researcher.
 MedicalDaily previously reported on the outbreak's 485 cases as voters approved Amendment 3 , a property tax measure that could affect future mosquito control budgets. Since then, the state has added 39 local cases, and the weekly pace in Hillsborough has dropped to less than half its September peak.
 Cooler Nights and a Mosquito That Lives Indoors
 Dr. Nicole Iovine, UF Health's chief epidemiologist, said lower temperatures make mosquitoes less active, but "you need at least one night of a good freeze" to actually kill off the population, according to a weather report on the incoming cold front. She believes people who arrived while infected may have passed the virus to local mosquitoes, which then spread it in Tampa Bay.
 Aedes aegypti bites mainly during the day and often lives in and around homes, breeding in small amounts of water in flowerpot saucers, buckets, tires, and toys. Cooler weather slows its breeding and biting, but Florida's mild winters can allow some adults to survive and stay active during warm spells, and eggs can survive for months in dry containers.
 Other researchers have made a similar point. John Drake, an infectious disease ecologist, wrote in Forbes that cooler November nights would probably do more to end the outbreak than aerial spraying. That is a projection, not a forecast of when cases will stop.
 Spraying Continues Under the Emergency Order
 County Administrator Bonnie Wise extended Hillsborough's local state of emergency through Nov. 12. The order was first issued Sept. 24.
 Because surveillance still detects dengue virus in mosquitoes in many neighborhoods, crews are increasing air and ground treatments. Paolo Pecora, a senior environmental scientist with Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services, has said crews target breeding areas for larvae and treat adult mosquitoes at night while they are flying in search of blood meals.
 A lower weekly count also lags behind infections. Symptoms can take up to two weeks to appear, testing and reporting take more time, and most infected people have mild symptoms or none, so official numbers likely understate how many people were infected.
 Protecting Households as Temperatures Drop
 The people most at risk of severe dengue are those who have had dengue before, infants, pregnant women, and older adults with chronic conditions . A second infection with a different type of the virus can be more dangerous than the first.
 Residents can empty and scrub containers that hold water at least weekly, keep screens repaired, wear long sleeves outdoors, and use repellent with DEET or picaridin. Warm afternoons during a cool spell can still bring biting mosquitoes, especially since Aedes aegypti bites mostly during the day.
 Dengue often starts with high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, and muscle and joint pain. Anyone with symptoms should see a clinician and avoid ibuprofen and aspirin, which can raise bleeding risk. Severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding from the gums or nose, or extreme tiredness can appear as fever fades and need emergency care.
 Uninsured residents with symptoms can contact the Florida Department of Health in Hillsborough County for testing guidance. The state posts county counts in its weekly arbovirus surveillance reports , and MedicalDaily will report whether the slowdown holds and whether the county lets its emergency order lapse.
 Developing Story Timeline
 Nov. 6, 2026: Weekly data show 22 new Hillsborough cases for Oct. 25 to 31, the lowest since mid-August, and 524 statewide. The county's emergency order is extended through Nov. 12.
 Sept. 24, 2026: Hillsborough declares a local state of emergency.
 Sept. 18, 2026: Florida confirms the year's first dengue death, a Tampa woman.

 Key Questions Answered
 How many dengue cases does Hillsborough County have? 407 locally acquired cases since July through Oct. 31.
 Is the outbreak slowing? Hillsborough added 22 cases in the latest week, its lowest since mid-August, but virus activity continues.
 Will cold weather end the outbreak? Cooler weather makes mosquitoes less active, but a UF Health expert said a hard freeze would be needed to kill them off.
 How many cases are there statewide? 524 locally acquired cases and 382 travel-associated cases this year.
 Is the emergency order still in effect? Yes. Hillsborough extended it through Nov. 12.
 What are dengue warning signs? Severe belly pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, and extreme tiredness. Seek emergency care.
